DocumentationNarrative.Title: Adapters

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
# AdventureWorks full BI stack
The load SQL uses explicit casts where SQL aliases or monetary types cross into different destination contracts. Raw integer fields remain integers. All 120 scripts have regenerated schema-aware Binding against the extracted SQL Server contracts; conversion-graph reachability cannot approve an unconverted expression.
The [conversion alignment](https://github.com/jimmy-zhao-tainio/meta-bi/blob/main/Demos/AdventureWorksBiStackDemo/CONVERSION-REVIEW.md) explains the corrected defaults, load casts, catalog ownership and the mesh's input/output path conventions.
## A complete BI stack built by an agent
The AdventureWorks stack was fully designed and built by an agent using the public Meta and meta-bi command-line tools. Its starting inputs were a live `AdventureWorks2022` database and a short [business request](https://github.com/jimmy-zhao-tainio/meta-bi/blob/main/Demos/AdventureWorksBiStackDemo/BUSINESS-REQUIREMENTS.md) for sales trends, channel and product analysis, geography, salesperson quotas, and visible data-quality risks.
The agent made the architectural decisions that turn those inputs into a BI system. It selected sales order, sales line, and salesperson quota as separate fact grains; kept tax and freight at order grain; created shared date, product, geography, customer, channel, and salesperson dimensions; derived the Online/Store channel from source evidence; and declined to publish gross margin because AdventureWorks lacks complete historical cost coverage.
The implementation is preserved as models rather than summarized after the fact. Every generated workspace was created through its owning CLI. The demo's MetaMesh workspace names 28 participating workspaces, 29 operations, and 614 ordered executable steps covering discovery, model authoring, conversion, deployment, transformation import and binding, pipeline construction, execution, verification, and analytical deployment. The generated results are checked in alongside that construction record.
## What the agent built
Each product owns a concrete part of the resulting stack:
| Engineering concern | AdventureWorks result | Modeled capability | | --- | --- | --- | | Discover the live source | 6 schemas, 71 tables, 20 views, 744 fields, and 90 relationships | `meta-schema` extracts a reviewable `MetaSchema` source contract. | | Preserve source history | 71 Raw hubs, 90 links, 71 satellites, and 341 satellite attributes | `meta-datavault-raw` and `meta-convert` turn the source contract into `MetaRawDataVault`, then into 232 deployable `MetaSql` tables through an explicit implementation model. | | Establish business meaning | 14 Business hubs, 19 links, 14 satellites, stable business names, and the Online/Store derivation | `meta-datavault-business` authors `MetaBusinessDataVault` concepts separately from the source-shaped Raw layer. | | Fix analytical grain | 3 facts, 8 conformed dimensions, 10 warehouse measures, 40 dimension attributes, and 19 fact-to-dimension relationships | `meta-data-warehouse` authors `MetaDataWarehouse`; `meta-convert` projects it through an implementation model into an 11-table physical warehouse. | | Make transformations provable | 53 source-to-Raw, 47 Raw-to-Business, and 20 Business-to-warehouse transformations, all validated against the current contracts | `meta-transform-script` models the T-SQL program; Binding validates its resulting contracts through `MetaSchema` and the selected `MetaDataType` catalog. Casts are authored before Binding. | | Turn evidence into quality checks | 167 promoted checks, with 45 returning wanted review findings in the recorded sample run | `meta-data-quality` derives reviewable `MetaDataQuality` candidates and `meta-convert` emits executable quality SQL. | | Operate the load | 3 pipelines containing 120 transformation tasks, plus one inferred orchestration plan over the same 120 tasks | `meta-pipeline` executes and records work; `meta-orchestration` derives and governs runtime dependencies. | | Publish portable analytics | 11 analytical tables, 72 attributes, 11 base measures, 3 hierarchies, and 19 relationships | `meta-analytics` carries engine-neutral `MetaAnalytics`; `meta-convert` and `meta-tabular` produce and operate the Analysis Services model. | | Model the conversion itself | One requirement and 24 executable Analytics-to-Tabular transformations | `meta-weave` executes a `MetaWeave` correspondence whose WeaveScript projection is readable and editable modeled transformation. |
## Prerequisites
- the `meta` and `meta-bi` CLIs on `PATH`; - a local SQL Server instance with `AdventureWorks2022` restored; - permission to create the four demo-owned databases; - Analysis Services Tabular only when running the optional Tabular deployment and processing operations.
`SOURCE-SETUP.md` covers the source database. `prepare-adventureworks-db.ps1` can download and restore the official backup on a local development machine.
## Environment
The examples below use the local default SQL Server instance:
```powershell $env:AW_SOURCE_SQL = "Server=.;Database=AdventureWorks2022;Integrated Security=true;TrustServerCertificate=true;Encrypt=false" $env:AW_ADMIN_SQL = "Server=.;Database=master;Integrated Security=true;TrustServerCertificate=true;Encrypt=false" $env:AW_RDV_SQL = "Server=.;Database=AdventureWorksRawVault;Integrated Security=true;TrustServerCertificate=true;Encrypt=false" $env:AW_BDV_SQL = "Server=.;Database=AdventureWorksBusinessVault;Integrated Security=true;TrustServerCertificate=true;Encrypt=false" $env:AW_DW_SQL = "Server=.;Database=AdventureWorksAnalytics;Integrated Security=true;TrustServerCertificate=true;Encrypt=false" $env:AW_PIPELINE_SQL = "Server=.;Database=AdventureWorksMetaPipeline;Integrated Security=true;TrustServerCertificate=true;Encrypt=false" ```
## Build the stack
Run from the mesh workspace:
```powershell cd AdventureWorksBiStackDemo.MetaMesh
meta-mesh run --operation validate-source meta-mesh run --operation sync-source-schema
meta-mesh run --operation create-raw-vault meta-mesh run --operation deploy-raw-vault meta-mesh run --operation create-source-raw-transforms meta-mesh run --operation create-source-raw-pipeline
meta-mesh run --operation create-business-vault meta-mesh run --operation deploy-business-vault meta-mesh run --operation create-raw-business-transforms meta-mesh run --operation create-raw-business-pipeline
meta-mesh run --operation create-dimensional-warehouse meta-mesh run --operation deploy-dimensional-warehouse meta-mesh run --operation create-business-warehouse-transforms meta-mesh run --operation create-business-warehouse-pipeline
meta-mesh run --operation create-orchestration meta-mesh run --operation deploy-pipeline-runtime meta-mesh run --operation create-data-quality meta-mesh run --operation deploy-data-quality meta-mesh run --operation create-analytics meta-mesh run --operation create-tabular ```
The three transform boundaries are strictly bound to modeled source and target schemas before their pipelines are authored. Orchestration is inferred from those pipeline tasks and binding effects.
Binding and execution explicitly select the mesh's `data-type` workspace through `--data-type-workspace`; omission loads the packaged authored workspace. Schema generation accepts separate catalog and conversion workspace options; this demo currently omits those options and uses the packaged workspaces. It authors its required casts directly in load SQL, so it does not need an `apply-conversions` step.
Workspace references identify inputs that must exist when an operation starts. Operations address their generated destinations through paths under the mesh root, so checked-in generated outputs are not prerequisites for regeneration. Run the operations in the documented order so each consuming operation has its inputs.
Warehouse deployment selects `deploy-plan --schema dw`. The manifest records this scope and deployment checks the same scoped live fingerprint. Separately deployed `dq` views are preserved. Omitting `--schema` retains database-wide reconciliation.
## Run and verify
Execute the inferred graph across all three pipelines, then reconcile the result to the source:
```powershell meta-mesh run --operation run-etl meta-mesh run --operation verify-stack ```
For an inspected layer-by-layer run, use `load-raw-vault`, `load-business-vault`, and `load-dimensional-warehouse` instead of `run-etl`.
The verification operation checks Raw and Business Vault counts, warehouse fact grains, source-to-warehouse measures, native Raw product types and exact values, deployed Data Quality results, and the latest task-level pipeline evidence. The live alignment loaded 31,465 orders, 121,317 lines and 163 quota rows through 120 successful tasks. The recorded Data Quality result is **167 promoted checks, 45 with findings**. Those findings are wanted review evidence, as explained below. `verify-stack` executes the deployed review once and reports the total checks, checks with findings and per-family finding groups. Findings do not automatically fail verification. Missing checks, SQL execution errors and failures in the other reconciliations still fail the operation.
## Data Quality findings
The demo retains the full promoted review pack and its findings. Returned rows identify situations to inspect; they do not automatically establish a faulty transformation. The reviewed sample result is:
| Check family | Checks with findings | Observed situation | | --- | ---: | --- | | JoinMultiplicityExplosion | 14 | Repeated use of lookup keys, including multiple lines per order | | OutputDuplicateRisk | 14 | The same join-key groupings, reviewed alongside actual output grains | | JoinOrphan | 12 | Related records unused by the consuming side, such as products never ordered | | OuterJoinNullExpansion | 5 | Missing relationships corresponding to nullable source references |
These are **45 nonempty checks**, not 45 bad records or 45 confirmed transform defects. Independent source comparisons explain the returned groups; forward reference probes found no missing lookups or duplicate applicable lookup keys, and the fact grains were verified separately. The checks and findings remain visible. The counts describe this recorded sample run, not general acceptance thresholds or permission to ignore future differences.
Inspect the findings on the local SQL Server instance:
```sql SELECT * FROM [AdventureWorksAnalytics].[dq].[v_DataQualityReview] WHERE COALESCE([ResultRowCount], [RowsReturned], 0) <> 0 ORDER BY [ResultRowCount] DESC, [CandidateId]; ```
`ReviewQuery` contains SQL for drilling into each check. See [DQ-REVIEW.md](https://github.com/jimmy-zhao-tainio/meta-bi/blob/main/Demos/AdventureWorksBiStackDemo/DQ-REVIEW.md) for the individual findings and supporting probes. The former expectation of no findings is superseded by this interpretation; the verifier does not hardcode 45 as an allowed-failure threshold. MetaDataQuality changes and production-scale execution/dashboard work are deferred; no checks are removed, suppressed or changed for this demo.
The final SQL alignment verification passed through the modeled `verify-stack` operation. Independent source comparisons found zero missing, extra or changed selected business rows across the eight reviewed warehouse outputs, including binary comparison of text. All 120 scripts were rebound against the selected catalog, and the latest task evidence contains 53, 47 and 20 successful tasks for the three pipelines. The demo mesh tour repeated the complete SQL load, stack verification, Tabular deployment and full processing on local services.
## Tabular runtime
The MetaAnalytics and MetaTabular workspaces are complete without Analysis Services. The runtime operations target the local `.\TABULAR` instance and deploy the model as `AdventureWorksSales`:
```powershell meta-mesh run --operation deploy-tabular meta-mesh run --operation process-tabular ```
`deploy-tabular` replaces the target database and deploys metadata without processing. `process-tabular` performs the full refresh. `drop-tabular` removes the deployed database.
The deployment operation also grants the local `NT Service\MSOLAP$TABULAR` service account read access to `AdventureWorksAnalytics`. The verified deployment contains 11 tables, 72 columns, 11 measures, and 19 relationships and completes a full refresh on `.\TABULAR`. A direct model query returns Sales Amount `109846381.425`, Total Due `123216786.1159`, and Quota Amount `95714000`, matching the relational verification.
The demo mesh tour repeated deployment and full processing. Independent queries compare these three measures with their source SQL totals.
## Cleanup
```powershell meta-mesh run --operation cleanup ```
Cleanup drops `AdventureWorksRawVault`, `AdventureWorksBusinessVault`, `AdventureWorksAnalytics`, and `AdventureWorksMetaPipeline`, then removes transient pipeline execution evidence under `Runs\ops\RunArtifacts`. It keeps the checked-in modeled workspaces. It does not remove the source database or an external Tabular database.

DocumentationNarrative.Body: Command-line tools for BI modeling, conversion, validation, and execution.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: CLI

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Demo meshes are authored workflows with different purposes. AdventureWorks exercises the integrated SQL/Tabular stack. Focused Pipeline, Orchestration, SQL corpus, Data Quality and Multidimensional examples cover additional statement types, failure branches and generation boundaries. Successful metadata deployment without processing is not an execution proof.
MetaMesh preflight checks declared workspace references before an operation begins. A workspace reference therefore identifies an available input. Creation steps address their new destinations through output paths under the mesh root. Within an operation that produces and consumes an artifact, later steps can use that output path. The invoked owning CLI validates and creates the artifact. No empty placeholder workspace is needed solely to satisfy preflight.
The Analytics authoring example separates cleanup, prepare-workspaces and author-analytics-model. Preparation creates the real empty model workspace; the authoring operation then populates it. The generation examples retain their own coherent operation boundaries and use output paths for artifacts produced inside an operation. Run operations in their documented order.
Mesh environment tokens such as {env:DEMO_SQL} supply the variable name for CLI options such as --connection-env. They do not interpolate the value into literal --server or --database-name arguments. Use the authored local SSAS target or change its step arguments through meta-mesh.
MetaTransformScriptConversionCliIntegration demonstrates integer-width normalization with a local catalog and authored conversion workspace. It applies a CAST snippet into a separate TransformScript workspace, independently binds it and executes through Pipeline on SQL Server. Changing only the authored snippet to CONVERT produces different SQL and repeats the same value checks. Unicode text, SQL NULL and empty strings are checked explicitly. The original script is preserved.
The conversion operation owns conversion application. Binding checks the resulting SQL types and facets; it neither selects snippets nor approves an unconverted expression through a conversion graph. Pipeline executes the validated result. Existing expression-typing and conversion destination limits still apply.
The AdventureWorks warehouse deploy-plan explicitly selects schema dw, preserving its separately deployed dq review pack. The demo retains all 167 promoted checks and their wanted findings; it does not change check eligibility to obtain a pass.
The [demo index](https://github.com/jimmy-zhao-tainio/meta-bi/blob/main/Demos/README.md) lists each example's useful coverage. The TPC-DS-derived corpus has 99 SQL Server-compatible view definitions and a regenerate-schema mesh operation. SourceSchema.sql supplies the 24 source tables. Generation compiles all views on SQL Server, extracts their output metadata, verifies all 1,040 columns and adapts the 99 output views to modeled table contracts through the owning CLIs. The checked-in SchemaWS is reproducible, with generation evidence and its previous version preserved. The strict Binding cases report 7 passes and 92 incomplete-type-evidence failures against the regenerated fixture. Query values over a populated TPC-DS dataset remain unverified. The Orchestration example uses nonempty source rows and exact output checks, including Unicode and an empty string. The focused Pipeline example verifies all five target tables and their audit defaults.
The corpus tour checks canonical SQL re-export byte for byte. The additional full MetaSql projection comparison remains a separate, slow diagnostic with no completed result in this tour. See the [corpus limitations](https://github.com/jimmy-zhao-tainio/meta-bi/blob/main/Demos/MetaTransformScriptTpcDsCliIntegration/CURRENT_GAPS.md) for its unverified status, the remaining Binding evidence gaps and the documented SQL Server adaptations.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Summary

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`IMetaSchemaDiscoveryAdapter` receives a provider-resolved connection reference and a system name, then returns a `MetaSchemaModel`. The provider describes the schemas, objects, fields, keys, and relationships available from that system using the normal MetaSchema contract. `MetaSchemaAdapterWorkspaceService` writes that model as an ordinary XML, C#, or SQL workspace through the normal workspace mapper.
Binding follows the existing meta-bi path. `TransformBindingWorkspaceService` binds a MetaTransformScript workspace against the discovered source and target MetaSchema workspaces and creates a validated MetaTransformBinding workspace. No adapter-specific binding path is introduced.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Discovery and binding

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`MetaSchemaAdapterExecutionService` loads the selected MetaSchema, MetaTransformScript, and MetaTransformBinding workspaces and uses MetaPipeline's existing execution resolver. For a row-producing transform it obtains an `IPipelineRowStreamSource` from `IMetaSchemaTransformAdapter` and an `IPipelineTargetWriteOperation` from `IMetaSchemaTargetWriteAdapter`. MetaPipeline checks the row shape, moves rows in batches, reports progress, and records the execution result. The execution service disposes the provider-owned target operation after the run.
For a mutating transform, the same service supplies the modeled contracts and selected identities to `IMetaSchemaMutationAdapter` and returns the provider's affected-row evidence.
Connection references are names resolved by the provider. Provider configuration, credentials, authentication, and physical I/O stay with the provider implementation.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Pipeline execution

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
A provider references `MetaSchema.Adapter`, implements `IMetaSchemaAdapter`, and adds only the capability interfaces it supports. Implementations translate the supported semantic forms using the transform model and binding evidence and report unsupported forms clearly. The application supplies configured adapter instances; provider package loading is left to the application host.
The meta-bi repository includes a test provider for tab-separated files in [`MetaSchemaAdapter/Tests/ExternalProvider`](https://github.com/jimmy-zhao-tainio/meta-bi/tree/main/MetaSchemaAdapter/Tests/ExternalProvider). Its integration test creates a MetaSchema workspace, imports a MetaTransformScript workspace, creates a validated MetaTransformBinding workspace through the existing binding service, evaluates the supported projection and predicate entities, and writes the result through MetaPipeline. The provider lives outside the MetaSchemaAdapter namespace and requires no changes to MetaSchema, MetaTransformBinding, or MetaPipeline.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Implementing a provider

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`MetaSchemaAdapter` is the provider boundary for systems outside the built-in SQL Server path. It lets a provider describe an external system as MetaSchema and supply the runtime capabilities it supports for bound transforms and pipeline writes.
The contract is split by capability. A read-only provider can offer discovery and row-producing transforms, while another provider may also support mutations or target inserts.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: MetaSchemaAdapter

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`IMetaSchemaTransformAdapter` creates an `IPipelineRowStreamSource` for a row-producing transform. `IMetaSchemaMutationAdapter` executes a bound mutating transform and returns the affected row count when the provider can report it.
The provider receives the MetaTransformScript semantic model together with the validated binding workspace and the identities of the selected transform and binding. The binding supplies resolved table sources, column references, rowsets, target evidence, and output shape. The provider works from those modeled entities rather than recovering meaning from emitted SQL text. Each provider implements the semantic forms its external system can execute.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Bound transforms

DocumentationNarrative.Body: Model references for the sanctioned BI metadata workspaces.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Models

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
| Area | Capability | | --- | --- | | Source structure and types | `MetaSchema` and its adapters provide a common contract for source objects, fields, keys and relationships. `MetaDataType` and `MetaDataTypeConversion` make type identities and conversion rules available during binding and generation. | | Data-store design | `MetaRawDataVault`, `MetaBusinessDataVault` and `MetaDataWarehouse` describe vault and dimensional structures. Separate implementation definitions apply physical conventions such as naming, keys, hashing, SQL types and indexes during conversion. | | Database deployment | `MetaSql` deployment plans record database differences, source and live fingerprints, and the approvals required for destructive changes. Deployment verifies the fingerprints before applying the recorded changes. | | Analytics | `MetaAnalytics` supplies shared analytical definitions for conversion to Tabular or Multidimensional targets. `MetaTabular` and `MetaMultiDimensional` add their respective calculations, security, partitions and tools for deployment, processing and queries. |
The [AdventureWorks example](https://github.com/jimmy-zhao-tainio/meta-bi/tree/main/Demos/AdventureWorksBiStackDemo) shows one possible arrangement: source discovery, Raw and Business Vaults, a dimensional warehouse and Tabular analytics, with quality checks and load orchestration. Its workspaces and build operations are included in the repository.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Other capabilities

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Across a large transformation estate, the same joins recur in different contexts. `MetaDataQuality` follows them through CTEs and derived queries and consolidates recurring patterns, retaining the transformations and occurrences behind each one.
From that structure it derives candidate checks for orphaned joins, null expansion, multiplicity growth and duplicate output. Review can focus on shared patterns and their reach across the system. Promoted candidates become executable SQL checks, with a review dashboard and an operational record of runs and findings. This connects quality investigation to the transformation logic that prompted it.

DocumentationNarrative.Title: Reference

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`MetaOrchestration` derives producer-consumer dependencies across pipelines from the reads and writes captured during binding. Load order follows those dependencies, supplemented by explicit ordering and locking policies.
Execution releases tasks as their prerequisites are satisfied and locks become available, allowing independent paths to run concurrently. Planning and run records cover tasks, locks, attempts, retries and failure branches. `MetaPipeline` performs the underlying work and records task results, row and batch counts, timings and failures.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Automatic orchestration

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Meta-BI provides models and tools for designing, building and running BI systems using a model-first principle. Source structures, data-store designs, transformations and analytical definitions supply the information used to generate, validate and operate the system.
`MetaMesh` brings these components together into a working system. It records the participating workspaces, commands and ordered steps as named operations for construction, deployment, execution and verification. An operation can build an environment, deploy one target or verify one layer. The construction process is maintained alongside the design, and its workspace and command references can be validated before execution.
Conversions connect the stages. `meta-convert` provides established conversion paths, while `MetaWeave` expresses correspondences and transformations between workspace contracts. These steps can be combined in a mesh to suit the project's architecture.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Overview

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`MetaTransformScript` exposes supported T-SQL as structured statements, queries and expressions. Transformation logic can be inspected and changed programmatically, including logic inside CTEs and derived queries, then emitted again as semantically equivalent code.
`MetaTransformBinding` resolves object and field references against source and target schemas, checks output shape and type compatibility, and records reads and writes. The resulting binding feeds quality analysis, execution and orchestration. Reusable transform patterns keep shared definitions separate from the SQL fragments supplied for each use.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Transformations

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`meta-sql deploy-plan --schema dw` declares one physical SQL Server schema as the deployment's desired-state boundary. All source tables, views, functions and stored procedures must belong to that schema. The empty implicit dbo schema in a SQL workspace is permitted.
The manifest stores this selection in `DeployManifest.ManagedSchemaName`. Deployment reads the saved scope; it has no independent override. Live extraction and live fingerprint validation use the same schema. A warehouse deployment scoped to dw preserves separately deployed dq objects, including changes made to them after planning. Changes inside dw still invalidate a stale manifest.
Without --schema, reconciliation remains database-wide. A database-wide manifest describes the complete desired database and may remove objects omitted from its source contract.
The single-schema path rejects inbound and outbound cross-schema foreign keys during planning and again before execution. Filtered extraction cannot represent those dependencies completely; they require a database-wide contract. SQL Server continues to enforce SQL module dependencies. Deployment retains statement-by-statement execution and is not atomic across statements.
Schema spelling must agree with the source contract. The selected MetaDataType catalog, source fingerprint and destructive table/column approvals retain their existing roles. Regenerate older manifests after updating the manifest model.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: SQL deployment ownership scope

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
For a packaged release, extract the archive and run `install-meta.exe`. Keep the extracted directory layout intact. The installer adds the tools to your user `PATH`; open a new terminal and run `meta help`.
A framework-dependent package needs the .NET 8 runtime. A self-contained package includes it.
To build from source, use the .NET 8 SDK and run these commands from the repository root:
```powershell dotnet build Metadata.Framework.sln dotnet run --project Meta\Cli\Meta.Cli.csproj -- help ```
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Install and run

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
You can author and change a model and its instances in any supported representation:
- **XML** expresses the model and its instances in deterministic files to review, branch and version in Git. - **SQL** expresses the model through tables, columns and foreign keys, with instances stored as rows. You can query and manage the metadata relationally, with database constraints enforcing its structure. - **C#** expresses the model through classes, properties and references, with instances represented as objects. Applications get typed access through readable, writable source.
Meta guarantees isomorphism across its supported XML, SQL and C# representations: conversion preserves the model, record identities, property values and relationships. This allows you to choose a representation to suit the work and move between them as your tools and workflow require. You can convert the model alone or include its instances.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Files, database tables and application code

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
The repository contains five command-line tools:
| Tool | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `meta` | Create, inspect, query and change models and their instances. | | `meta-cli` | Define a tool's commands and options in a model, with shared parsing, help and runtime binding. | | `meta-weave` | Define correspondences between models and execute transformations that populate a target workspace. | | `meta-docs` | Combine authored explanations with generated command and model reference material, then render the documentation. | | `meta-mesh` | Record the workspaces and ordered commands needed for a repeatable repository workflow. |
[Meta-BI](https://github.com/jimmy-zhao-tainio/meta-bi) builds on this foundation with models and tools for BI engineering.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: The foundation tools

DocumentationNarrative.Body: Meta is a foundation for building tools and systems around metadata models. You can define a model, query and edit its instances, refactor its structure together with the affected data, and use its definitions to drive transformations and tools.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Meta

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
A model defines types, properties and relationships. For example, a model could define `Country` and `City`, their names, and a relationship linking each city to its country. Sweden and Stockholm are **instances** of those types. Meta calls a model and its instances a **workspace**.
Use `meta` to inspect models, query records, follow relationships, edit values and compare workspaces. Its refactoring commands change model definitions together with the affected records—for example, turning a property into a relationship. This lets you evolve how information is structured while carrying the existing data through the change.
Models also provide the definitions used by other tools. A model can describe a command interface, a correspondence between two models, or the workspaces and steps in a repository workflow. The foundation tools use these definitions to expose commands, transform data, generate reference documentation and execute repeatable operations.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Working with models and instances

DocumentationNarrative.Body: The `workspace.meta` file identifies the workspace's representation and storage configuration. Commands use the current directory by default; pass `--workspace <path>` to select another workspace. Run `meta help` to list commands, or `meta help <command>` for their arguments and options.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Selecting a workspace
